title: Who Needs You First?
task: Which patient should move to the front of the line?
scene: Three patients arrive at almost the same time. Ava sits very still and breathes hard. Ben can walk, but his ankle hurts. Maya has an itchy patch on her arm. One exam room is free. Hospitals do not always help people in the order they arrive. Some problems stay the same for an hour. Others get worse fast. Picking who goes first is called triage.
takeaway: Doctors use urgency, not first-come-first-served order, when several patients need help at once.
why: Breathing brings oxygen into the body. Every part needs it, all the time. So when breathing is hard, the whole body is in trouble fast. A sore ankle hurts and stays about the same. An itchy patch stays about the same too. You go to the one that can get worse quickest.
assumes: your body needs air all the time

choices: Ava, because breathing trouble can affect the whole body quickly.
Ben, because you can see his injury and Ava is sitting quietly.
Maya, because a rash might spread to other people in the room.
Whoever arrived first, so nobody waits longer than anybody else.
rebuttals: B. Ben, because you can see his injury and Ava is sitting quietly. — Ben can walk and talk. A hurt you can see is not always the one to fix first.
C. Maya, because a rash might spread to other people in the room. — An itchy patch can wait a little. Maya is breathing and talking just fine.
D. Whoever arrived first, so nobody waits longer than anybody else. — That is fair for a line at a shop. Here the sickest person goes first.
text.setup: Ava, Ben, and Maya • Emergency Department

equations.e: how far behind = what is needed − what was taken

title: Observation or Measurement?
task: Which item is a measurement?
scene: Luis says his belly hurts. You can see that he is awake and talking. A nurse checks his temperature with a thermometer. She counts his pulse too. All of it goes on his chart. But the clues are not all the same kind. Some you notice. Some the patient tells you. Some come from a tool, as a number.
takeaway: Doctors combine observations, patient stories, and measurements. They are different kinds of clues.
why: Clues come in three kinds. Some you see, like a worried face. Some the patient tells you, like where it hurts. Some come from a tool, as a number. A thermometer gives a number. That makes it a measurement. All three kinds are useful. Knowing which kind you have tells you how sure you can be.
assumes: a tool can give you a number

choices: Luis says his belly hurts.
Luis looks worried.
His temperature is 98.7°F.
He skipped breakfast.
rebuttals: A. Luis says his belly hurts. — Pain is important information, but it is something Luis reports, not a tool measurement.
B. Luis looks worried. — Looking worried is an observation.
D. He skipped breakfast. — Skipping breakfast is part of the story or history.

equations.e: beats in a minute = beats in 15 seconds × 4
equations.about: scaling a short count up to a rate

title: Your First Exam Room
task: Put these steps in the best order.
scene: Ben is here for his ankle check. The team has four things to do. Clean hands. Ben's story. A look at the ankle. A note for the next person.
takeaway: Each step in a hospital routine is there to make the next one work.
why: Each step makes the next one work. Hands come first. What is on them goes on to Ben. His story comes next. It tells you where to look. Then you look. Then you write it down, so the next person knows what you saw.
assumes: germs can travel on hands
answerText: 1. Clean your hands, so nothing from the last patient travels to Ben. 2. Ask Ben what happened, and where it hurts most. 3. Look at the ankle, using what Ben said to know where to look. 4. Write down the clues, so the next person sees what you saw.

cards: Clean your hands, so nothing from the last patient travels to Ben.
Ask Ben what happened, and where it hurts most.
Look closely at the sore ankle, and compare it with the other one.
Write down the clues, so the evening nurse sees what you saw.

title: Follow One Breath
task: Put the path of a breath in order.
scene: Priya takes a deep breath. She asks where the air goes. You have four picture cards: the nose and mouth, the windpipe, the lungs, and the blood.
takeaway: The lungs are the meeting place between outside air and the blood.
why: Air has to travel to get where it is needed. In through the nose or mouth. Down the windpipe. Into the lungs. Only then can oxygen move into the blood. The blood carries it to every part of the body. Knowing the path helps you guess where a problem might be.
assumes: air goes in through your nose and mouth
answerText: Air enters through the nose or mouth. -> Air moves down the windpipe. -> Air reaches the lungs. -> Oxygen moves into the blood to travel around the body.

cards: Air enters through the nose or mouth.
Air moves down the windpipe.
Air reaches the lungs.
Oxygen moves into the blood to travel around the body.

title: The Dusty-Room Clue
task: Which body system should the team focus on first?
scene: Noah helped clean a dusty storage room. Now he is wheezing. He can still talk. Each breath makes a small whistling sound. The team is with him. One clue by itself does not mean much. The useful question is which body part could make that clue. A whistle needs air squeezing through a narrow space. So the clue points somewhere.
takeaway: A clue is useful when you connect it to the body system that could produce it.
why: A whistle needs air squeezing through a narrow space. Noah makes that sound with every breath. So it is the breathing tubes that got narrow. That is what wheezing is. One clue on its own does not mean much. This one is useful because you can name the part that made it.
assumes: blowing through a small gap makes a whistle

choices: The breathing system — the airways and lungs.
The throat and voice box, because that is where whistling sounds are made.
The heart and blood vessels, because a whistle could be blood rushing.
The digestive system, because Noah breathed in dust and swallowed some.
rebuttals: B. The throat and voice box, because that is where whistling sounds are made. — The voice box makes talking sounds. This whistle comes with every breath, from lower down.
C. The heart and blood vessels, because a whistle could be blood rushing. — The heart makes a thump you hear with a stethoscope. It does not whistle when Noah breathes.
D. The digestive system, because Noah breathed in dust and swallowed some. — Dust may reach his stomach. A stomach does not make a sound with each breath.

equations.e: how far behind = what is needed − what was taken

title: Count the Breaths
task: 5 breaths in 15 seconds is about how many breaths in 60 seconds?
scene: Mrs. Grant is resting. The nurse counts 5 breaths in 15 seconds. She asks you for the one minute number. This is math practice only.
takeaway: Doctors often turn short counts into one-minute estimates.
why: One minute has four 15-second parts. So 5 breaths in 15 seconds is 5 four times, which is 20. Nurses count short blocks to save time. People also breathe differently when they know somebody is watching. So a short count is often the honest one.
assumes: a minute has 60 seconds

rebuttals: A. 10 — 10 would be only two groups of 5.
B. 15 — 15 would be three groups of 5.
D. 60 — 60 is the number of seconds in a minute, not the estimated number of breaths.

estimate.relationship: A minute has four fifteen-second parts. Breaths in a minute = breaths in fifteen seconds × 4.

equations.e: beats in a minute = beats in 15 seconds × 4
equations.about: scaling a short count up to a rate

equations.e: breaths in a minute = breaths in 15 seconds × 4

title: The Blood Loop
task: Put the simplified blood loop in order, starting at the heart.
scene: A heart model sits on the table. Four arrow cards lie beside it. The nurse says blood moves in a loop. Heart, lungs, heart, body, and back.
takeaway: Circulation is a loop, not a one-way trip.
why: Blood does not go one way and stop. It goes around and around. The heart pumps it to the lungs. In the lungs it picks up oxygen. The heart pumps it out to the body. Then it comes back. That is a loop, and it never stops all day or all night.
assumes: the heart is a pump
answerText: The heart pumps blood toward the lungs. -> In the lungs, blood picks up oxygen. -> The heart pumps oxygen-rich blood to the body. -> Blood returns from the body to the heart.

cards: The heart pumps blood toward the lungs.
In the lungs, blood picks up oxygen.
The heart pumps oxygen-rich blood to the body.
Blood returns from the body to the heart.

title: Pulse Math
task: 18 beats in 15 seconds is about how many beats in 60 seconds?
scene: Jordan is resting after the stairs. The therapist counts 18 beats in 15 seconds. She asks you for the one minute number. This is math practice only.
takeaway: A pulse is a clue that the heart is beating and moving blood.
why: One minute has four 15-second parts. So 18 beats in 15 seconds is 18 four times, which is 72. Each beat is one push of blood. You can feel that push with two fingers and a clock. It is one of the oldest checks in medicine.
assumes: a minute has 60 seconds

estimate.relationship: A minute has four fifteen-second parts. Beats in a minute = beats in fifteen seconds × 4.

equations.e: beats in a minute = beats in 15 seconds × 4
equations.about: scaling a short count up to a rate

title: Why the Faster Pulse?
task: What is the best explanation?
scene: Jordan's pulse was slow while he sat. It was fast right after the stairs. He feels fine now. The doctor asks you why it went up.
takeaway: Body systems work together. Muscles, lungs, blood, and heart all change during exercise.
why: Working muscles need more oxygen. Blood is what carries oxygen. So the heart pumps faster to get more blood to them. A pulse is not one fixed number for a person. It goes up and down all day. When one part of the body works harder, another part changes to help.
assumes: muscles work harder when you climb stairs

choices: Working muscles need more oxygen, so the heart moves blood faster.
The heart beats faster to help the body cool down after exercise.
Climbing stairs shakes the body, which makes the heartbeat easier to feel.
The pulse only seems faster because Jordan is paying attention to it.
rebuttals: B. The heart beats faster to help the body cool down after exercise. — Cooling is mostly the skin's job, with sweat. The faster pulse is about oxygen.
C. Climbing stairs shakes the body, which makes the heartbeat easier to feel. — Jordan is resting now, and it is still fast. Shaking would have stopped.
D. The pulse only seems faster because Jordan is paying attention to it. — The therapist counted it. A count is a real number, not a feeling.

equations.e: beats in a minute = beats in 15 seconds × 4
equations.about: scaling a short count up to a rate

title: Follow the Sandwich
task: Put the food journey in order.
scene: Owen has a paper sandwich card. He wants to know where it goes after he swallows. The dietitian hands you four organ cards and asks you to put them in order.
takeaway: Different organs have different jobs in one connected system.
why: Food is far too big for the body to use. It gets broken down in stages. The mouth chews it and wets it. It goes down the food tube. The stomach mixes it and breaks it down more. Then the small intestine takes the tiny bits into the blood. Each part does one piece of the job.
assumes: food gets chewed before you swallow it
answerText: The mouth chews food and mixes it with saliva. -> Food travels down the food tube to the stomach. -> The stomach mixes and breaks food down more. -> The small intestine takes many nutrients into the blood.

cards: The mouth chews food and mixes it with saliva.
Food travels down the food tube to the stomach.
The stomach mixes and breaks food down more.
The small intestine takes many nutrients into the blood.

title: Why Food Is Fuel
task: Nina ran all morning and has not eaten. Why does she feel shaky?
scene: Nina ran all morning and now she feels shaky. She has not eaten since breakfast. Her nurse asks you what her body has run out of.
takeaway: The body spends what it takes in, and spends it faster when it works harder.
why: Food is fuel. Your body breaks food down and uses the energy to move, to keep warm, and to think. Running uses a lot of energy fast. Nina ate at breakfast and then used it all up. When the fuel runs low, people feel shaky, tired, or grumpy. A snack puts the fuel back. This is why hospitals ask when someone last ate.
assumes: food gives your body energy

choices: Her body used up the energy from her food, and running uses more of it.
Her muscles got bigger from running, so they need more room.
She has too much water inside her from her drink bottle.
Shaky hands are only about being nervous, not about food.
rebuttals: Muscles do get stronger with exercise, but that takes weeks. It does not make you shaky today.
Water is important, and it carries no energy. You can drink plenty and still run out of fuel.
Feeling nervous can make hands shake too. Here she is hungry, and that is easy to fix.

title: Three Jobs, Three Organs
task: Which matching set is correct?
scene: Three cards each need one picture. Owen needs the part that starts breaking food up. Sam needs the part that mixes it. Nia needs the part that soaks it up.
takeaway: A body system works because specialized parts each do a piece of the job.
why: A body system works like a good team. Nobody does everything. The mouth chews, so the pieces get smaller. The stomach mixes and breaks them down more. The small intestine soaks up the tiny bits. Each part is built for its own job, and the order matters.
assumes: different body parts do different jobs

choices: Owen—mouth; Sam—stomach; Nia—small intestine
Owen—stomach; Sam—mouth; Nia—small intestine
Owen—mouth; Sam—small intestine; Nia—stomach
Owen—mouth; Sam—stomach; Nia—large intestine
rebuttals: B. Owen—stomach; Sam—mouth; Nia—small intestine — Owen and Sam are swapped. Chewing starts in the mouth, not the stomach.
C. Owen—mouth; Sam—small intestine; Nia—stomach — Sam and Nia are swapped. Mixing comes before soaking up.
D. Owen—mouth; Sam—stomach; Nia—large intestine — Only Nia is wrong. Most nutrients go in at the small intestine.
text.setup: Sam, Nia, and Owen • Pediatric Exam Room

equations.e: how far behind = what is needed − what was taken

title: The Thirsty Player
task: What body need do these clues most strongly point to?
scene: Mateo just finished soccer. He is thirsty and his mouth is dry. The nurse says his urine looks darker than it was. The team is checking him.
takeaway: The body tells you when it is short of something, and thirst is one of those signals.
why: Water is in your blood, in every cell, and in your sweat. You lose some when you are active. Then the body gives signals. A dry mouth is one. Dark urine is another. Doctors read several signals together, because one on its own could mean lots of things. Two pointing the same way is stronger.
assumes: you sweat when you run around

choices: The body may need more water.
The body may need more food, because practice used up his energy.
The body may need more sleep after a long practice.
The body may be too warm and need to cool down.
rebuttals: B. The body may need more food, because practice used up his energy. — Being hungry is real. A dry mouth and dark urine are water clues, not food clues.
C. The body may need more sleep after a long practice. — Rest helps. Sleep does not make your mouth dry or your urine dark.
D. The body may be too warm and need to cool down. — Getting warm is part of it. He lost water in that sweat, and that is what the clues show.

title: The Drink Tracker
task: How many cups short of what her body lost is she?
scene: Mrs. Lee has a drink chart by her bed. It shows 2 cups in the morning, 1 cup at lunch, and 3 cups later. A wall chart says a body her size loses about 8 cups a day. This is a math problem, not drink advice.
takeaway: Water balance is what goes in measured against what goes out, not either one alone.
why: Six cups went in. About eight cups went out. That leaves her two cups short. The body loses water all day, even when you are still. So you count what goes in against what goes out. One number on its own does not tell you much.
assumes: you can add up a list of numbers

rebuttals: A. 4 — 4 leaves out two of the cups.
B. 5 — 5 is one cup too few.
D. 7 — 7 is one cup too many.

estimate.relationship: How far behind = what she needs − what she drank. Add the drinks up first.

equations.e: how far behind = what is needed − what was taken

title: What the Kidneys Do
task: Put the simplified pathway in order.
scene: Harper is looking at a model. It shows the kidneys and the bladder. She asks why both are in one system. The body always makes waste it cannot keep. The blood carries that waste. The kidneys are the filters that pull it out. But filtering never stops, and nobody can visit a bathroom all day. So the system also needs a place to hold it.
takeaway: Kidneys filter; the bladder stores.
why: Blood picks up waste from all over the body. It has to go somewhere. Blood flows through the kidneys. The kidneys take out waste and extra water. That makes urine. The urine moves to the bladder, which stores it until you go. Two organs, one path, different jobs.
assumes: your body makes waste it has to get rid of
answerText: Blood flows through the kidneys. -> The kidneys remove some wastes and extra water from the blood. -> That liquid becomes urine and moves toward the bladder. -> The bladder stores urine until it leaves the body.

cards: Blood flows through the kidneys.
The kidneys remove some wastes and extra water from the blood.
That liquid becomes urine and moves toward the bladder.
The bladder stores urine until it leaves the body.

equations.e: how far behind = what is needed − what was taken

title: Why Take an X-Ray?
task: Which hospital tool best matches that job?
scene: Eli fell off his bike. His wrist hurts and looks swollen. The doctor needs to know if a bone is broken. The bone is under the skin. Nobody can see it from outside. Hospitals have many tools. Each one answers a different question. Picking the right tool matters. The wrong tool answers a question nobody asked.
takeaway: Doctors choose tools based on the kind of clue they need.
why: You cannot see a bone by looking at an arm. An X-ray makes a picture of what is under the skin, and bones show up clearly in it. That is why it is the right tool here. A thermometer gives warmth. A stethoscope gives sound. Neither one shows a shape.
assumes: some things are hidden under the skin

choices: An X-ray image
A thermometer
A stethoscope
A tape measure, to record how swollen the wrist is
rebuttals: B. A thermometer — A thermometer tells you how warm someone is. It cannot show a bone.
C. A stethoscope — A stethoscope lets you hear the heart and lungs. Bones make no sound to listen for.
D. A tape measure, to record how swollen the wrist is — Measuring the swelling is useful. It still does not show what the bone is doing.

equations.e: how far behind = what is needed − what was taken

title: Skeleton Jobs
task: Which set is correct?
scene: The bone doctor has three cards to hand out. Rosa needs the part that protects the heart and lungs. Mr. Bell needs the part that holds up the back. Tess needs the place where bones meet and move. Bones do more than hold you up. They are not all the same shape. That is because they do not all do the same job.
takeaway: The skeleton supports, protects, and helps the body move.
why: Bones do more than one job. The rib cage is a cage, so it guards the heart and lungs inside it. The spine holds you up and guards the nerve cord running down your back. A joint is a place where two bones meet, and that is where you bend. Same material, three different jobs.
assumes: bones are hard and do not bend

choices: Rosa—rib cage; Mr. Bell—spine; Tess—joint
Rosa—spine; Mr. Bell—rib cage; Tess—joint
Rosa—rib cage; Mr. Bell—joint; Tess—spine
Rosa—skull; Mr. Bell—spine; Tess—joint
rebuttals: B. Rosa—spine; Mr. Bell—rib cage; Tess—joint — Rosa and Mr. Bell are swapped. The rib cage is the part that guards the chest.
C. Rosa—rib cage; Mr. Bell—joint; Tess—spine — Mr. Bell and Tess are swapped. A joint is where two bones meet and bend.
D. Rosa—skull; Mr. Bell—spine; Tess—joint — Only Rosa is wrong. The skull guards the brain, not the chest.
text.setup: Rosa, Mr. Bell, and Tess • Orthopedic Room

equations.e: how far behind = what is needed − what was taken

title: Possible Broken Bone
task: Put the safe hospital response in order.
scene: Eli's wrist may be hurt. He looks worried. In this game you do not fix it. You keep him safe and get the team what they need.
takeaway: The first action is the one that stops things getting worse; the rest can happen while it holds.
why: Keeping the wrist still comes first. It is the only step that stops more harm. All the rest can happen while you hold it still. Then you tell a grown-up, because help takes time to come. The note goes last. It writes down all of it.
assumes: moving something that is hurt can make it worse
answerText: 1. Stop Eli using the wrist, because moving a broken bone can damage what is around it. 2. Tell the nurse or doctor, so trained help is already coming. 3. Let the trained team examine the wrist and decide about an image. 4. Record what happened and what the team found.

cards: Stop Eli using the wrist, because moving a broken bone can damage what is around it.
Tell the nurse or doctor, so trained help is already coming.
Let the trained team examine the wrist and decide about an image.
Record what happened and what the team found.

title: Make the Hand Move
task: Put the movement pathway in order.
scene: Sophie wiggles her fingers. She asks how the message got there so fast. The therapist gives you four cards. Moving one finger takes a whole chain. First a decision. Then a message along a nerve. Then a muscle pulls. Then a bone moves at a joint. Therapists think about this chain a lot. When movement fails, the chain shows where to look.
takeaway: One movement needs several parts of the body working in turn.
why: Moving takes four things in order. The brain decides. Nerves carry that message out to the muscles. The muscles tighten and pull. Bones move at the joints. Muscles can only pull, never push, which is why they come in pairs. Nothing moves until the message gets there.
assumes: your brain is in charge of your body
answerText: The brain decides to move the hand. -> Nerves carry the message toward the muscles. -> Muscles tighten and pull. -> Bones move at the joints.

cards: The brain decides to move the hand.
Nerves carry the message toward the muscles.
Muscles tighten and pull.
Bones move at the joints.

equations.e: how far behind = what is needed − what was taken

title: Tired Muscles
task: Why is rest a sensible next step in this scene?
scene: Amara has done the same gentle motion many times. Her arm feels tired now. Nothing hurts sharply. There is no new injury. The therapist stops the set and lets her rest. Muscles use energy every time they pull. Doing one motion over and over uses it up fast. Tired is not the same as hurt. Therapists plan rest for that reason.
takeaway: Body tissues can change their activity depending on what the body is doing.
why: Muscles use energy when they work. Do the same thing lots of times and they run low. Then they feel tired and weak. That is normal, and it is not the same as being hurt. Rest lets them fill back up. In therapy the rest is part of the plan, not a sign to stop.
assumes: you get tired after doing something over and over

choices: Muscles can get tired after repeated work and need recovery time.
The arm is injured, and rest is how an injury heals.
Muscles only grow while a person is resting, so the set is finished.
Tiredness means the therapy is not working and should be changed.
rebuttals: B. The arm is injured, and rest is how an injury heals. — Nothing here says he is hurt. Tired and hurt are not the same thing.
C. Muscles only grow while a person is resting, so the set is finished. — Rest does help. That is not a reason to stop in the middle of the plan.
D. Tiredness means the therapy is not working and should be changed. — Getting tired is what is supposed to happen. It means the muscle is working.

title: Therapy Sets
task: How many leg lifts are in 3 sets of 5?
scene: Mr. Diaz is doing gentle leg lifts. His therapist picked 3 sets of 5. The therapist chose the plan, not you. Therapy uses sets because short rests help muscles. Counting in groups is also easier to track. A nurse can count to five while talking. Fifteen is harder. Groups of the same size are what multiplying is for.
takeaway: Repeated sets are groups, so multiplication helps count them quickly.
why: There are 3 sets, and each set has 5 lifts. So it is 5 three times, which is 15. This is why therapy is counted in sets. Counting the total helps the team see if it is getting easier or harder from one day to the next.
assumes: a set is a group of the same thing

rebuttals: A. 8 — 8 comes from adding 3 + 5.
B. 10 — 10 is only two groups of 5.
D. 35 — 35 joins the digits instead of multiplying.

estimate.relationship: Total lifts = number of sets × lifts in each set.

title: The Body's Slow Messages
task: Theo grew four centimetres, mostly while asleep. What told his bones to do that?
scene: Theo is eleven and has grown four centimetres since spring. His chart shows he grew most while he was asleep. He wants to know who told his bones to grow.
takeaway: The body sends slow chemical messages, and some of them tell the body to grow.
why: The body has two ways to send messages. Nerves are fast, like pulling your hand off something hot. Hormones are slow. They are chemicals that travel in the blood and can take hours or years to finish their job. Growth hormone is one of them, and the body makes most of it during sleep. That is why Theo grew while he was asleep, and why sleep is part of growing.
assumes: your blood carries things all around your body

choices: A chemical message called a hormone, which travels in the blood and works slowly.
A nerve message from his brain, which travels fast and stops right away.
The food in his stomach, which pushes his bones longer.
Nothing told them. Bones grow at the same speed all the time.
rebuttals: Nerve messages are fast and short. Growing takes months, so it is not a nerve doing it.
Food gives the body what it needs to build bone. It does not push bones longer.
Children grow faster at some ages than others, which is a sign something is telling them when.

title: Touch, Think, Move
task: Put the stages in order.
scene: Lily touches something very cold. She pulls her hand back fast. The brain doctor shows four cards. It felt like one instant to Lily. It was really a sequence. Something was noticed. A message travelled. The brain understood it. A muscle moved. Each stage takes a tiny bit of time. So the order can be worked out.
takeaway: The nervous system helps the body notice changes and respond.
why: You cannot answer something you have not noticed yet. So the skin senses the cold first. Nerves carry that message inward. The nervous system works out what it means. Then a message goes back out to the muscles and the hand moves. It feels like one thing. It is really four, in order.
assumes: you pull your hand back from something cold
answerText: Skin senses the cold touch. -> Nerves carry a message inward. -> The nervous system processes the signal. -> A message goes to muscles and the hand moves.

cards: Skin senses the cold touch.
Nerves carry a message inward.
The nervous system processes the signal.
A message goes to muscles and the hand moves.

title: After the Head Bump
task: Who should the hospital team check first?
scene: Three children come in after playground falls. Arjun bumped his head. Now he seems confused. He has trouble answering simple questions. Bea has a small scrape on her elbow. Cole has a sore finger and talks normally. Clues about how someone thinks and answers matter a lot. The brain is hard to check from outside. Always tell an adult after a head bump.
takeaway: In real life, children should tell an adult right away after a significant head injury or new concerning symptoms.
why: You can see a scrape and you cannot see a brain. So a change in how somebody thinks is the clue that matters after a head bump. Arjun is mixed up, and that is new. Bea's scrape can be cleaned. Cole's finger can wait for a picture. Only one of these could be getting worse right now.
assumes: your brain is inside your head

choices: Arjun, because confusion after a head injury can be an important warning sign.
Bea, because her scrape is bleeding and can be cleaned quickly.
Cole, because a sore finger might be broken and needs an image.
Arjun last, because he is walking and talking on his own.
rebuttals: B. Bea, because her scrape is bleeding and can be cleaned quickly. — A scrape does need cleaning. Bleeding you can see is not the same as danger.
C. Cole, because a sore finger might be broken and needs an image. — A picture of the finger can wait. A change in how someone thinks cannot.
D. Arjun last, because he is walking and talking on his own. — Walking and talking is good news. Being mixed up after a head bump is still a warning.
text.setup: Arjun and two other children • Observation Room

title: Which Test Fits the Clue?
task: Which tool best matches Mina’s clue?
scene: Mina says the board looks blurry from far away. Her book looks fine. The eye doctor wants to start simple. A test is really a question. A good first test asks what the patient just asked. Here that is what Mina can see at different sizes. Starting with the matching test saves time. It also points at what to do next.
takeaway: The best test depends on the question you are trying to answer.
why: Match the tool to the clue. The clue here is about seeing, so you want the tool made for eyes, and that is the eye chart. A hearing test checks ears. A stethoscope hears sounds. An X-ray shows bones. Every one of them is a good tool. Only one answers this question.
assumes: different tools check different things

choices: An eye chart
A hearing test in the sound booth
A stethoscope for listening to the heart
An X-ray for bones
rebuttals: B. A hearing test in the sound booth — A hearing test checks the ears. The clue here is about seeing.
C. A stethoscope for listening to the heart — A stethoscope hears sounds inside the body. Eyes make no sound.
D. An X-ray for bones — An X-ray shows bones. It does not show how well someone reads a page.

title: Match the Sense
task: Which body-part match is best?
scene: The team has three clue cards. Mina has blurry vision. Caleb has trouble hearing a tone. Mrs. Patel feels unsteady when she turns her head. Each sense starts with a part built to catch one kind of signal. Light. Sound. Movement. Here is the surprise. One organ can hold more than one of those jobs.
takeaway: One organ can have more than one job; the ear helps with both hearing and balance.
why: Eyes take in light, and that is how we see. Ears take in sound, and that is how we hear. But the inner ear does a second job too. It tells the brain which way is up. That is why a problem in there can make somebody dizzy even when their hearing is fine.
assumes: your eyes see and your ears hear

choices: Mina—eyes; Caleb—ears; Mrs. Patel—inner-ear balance system
Mina—eyes; Caleb—inner-ear balance system; Mrs. Patel—ears
Mina—eyes; Caleb—ears; Mrs. Patel—leg muscles
Mina—eyes; Caleb—throat; Mrs. Patel—inner-ear balance system
rebuttals: B. Mina—eyes; Caleb—inner-ear balance system; Mrs. Patel—ears — Caleb and Mrs. Patel are swapped. Hearing sound is the ears' main job.
C. Mina—eyes; Caleb—ears; Mrs. Patel—leg muscles — Only Mrs. Patel is wrong. Legs hold you up, and the inner ear tells you which way is up.
D. Mina—eyes; Caleb—throat; Mrs. Patel—inner-ear balance system — Only Caleb is wrong. The throat makes sound. The ears take it in.
text.setup: Mina, Caleb, and Mrs. Patel • Hearing Booth

title: From Light to Picture
task: Put the simplified vision pathway in order.
scene: Jules wants to know how light becomes a picture. The brain doctor lays out four cards. Eyes do not really see on their own. They catch light and turn it into signals. The picture is put together later, in the brain. That is why seeing is a team job. Knowing the stages tells you where a problem could be.
takeaway: Seeing is a team job between the eyes, nerves, and brain.
why: Seeing is not one step. Light comes into the eye. The back of the eye picks up the pattern. A nerve carries that to the brain. The brain works out what it is. So the eye collects, and the brain understands. A problem could be at any point along that line.
assumes: you need light to see
answerText: Light enters the eye. -> The back of the eye detects the light pattern. -> A nerve carries signals toward the brain. -> The brain uses the signals to make sense of what is seen.

cards: Light enters the eye.
The back of the eye detects the light pattern.
A nerve carries signals toward the brain.
The brain uses the signals to make sense of what is seen.

title: How a Scrape Heals
task: Put the steps of healing in order.
scene: Ella has a small scrape. The team cleaned it and covered it. She asks what her body will do next. Skin is not a wrapper. It is living tissue. It fixes itself in stages, in the same order every time. First the bleeding stops. Then the cleanup. Then rebuilding. Knowing the stages tells you what is normal.
takeaway: Skin is living tissue that can repair many small injuries.
why: Healing goes in stages. First the skin is broken open. Then the blood clots and closes the gap. Then a scab forms and covers it like a lid. Under that lid, new skin grows. The body shuts the door first and does the repairs after. That is why picking a scab sets it back.
assumes: a cut stops bleeding on its own after a while
answerText: The skin barrier is broken by the scrape. -> Blood clotting helps close the damaged area. -> A scab or protective covering forms while healing continues. -> New skin grows underneath as the area repairs.

cards: The skin barrier is broken by the scrape.
Blood clotting helps close the damaged area.
A scab or protective covering forms while healing continues.
New skin grows underneath as the area repairs.

title: Clean Team, Not DIY Doctor
task: Put the junior-doctor actions in order.
scene: You are the junior doctor in this game. Real wound care is a job for grown-ups. Your job is to keep things safe and in order.
takeaway: A scrape is a break in the barrier, so everything that touches it has to be clean.
why: Tell a grown-up first. Help takes time to come, and nothing else has to wait for it. Then clean your hands. A cut is a way in, and hands are how germs move. Then get the things they need. The grown-up cares for the cut. You keep the notes.
assumes: some jobs are for grown-ups
answerText: 1. Tell the nurse or doctor, so trained help starts on its way. 2. Clean your own hands, because hands carry germs better than anything else you touch with. 3. Let the trained adult clean and cover the scrape. 4. Record what happened, and watch for instructions.

cards: Tell the nurse or doctor, so trained help starts on its way.
Clean your own hands, because hands carry germs better than anything else you touch with.
Let the trained adult clean and cover the scrape.
Record what happened, and watch for instructions.

title: What Job Did the Skin Lose?
task: Which main skin job is most connected to this lesson?
scene: June was outside too long. Now she has a mild sunburn. The skin doctor explains what skin does. It keeps water in. It keeps germs out. It shields everything under it. Sunlight also carries a kind of light we cannot see. Too much of it can hurt skin cells. So the shield needs shade and sunscreen too.
takeaway: Skin protects the body, but the skin itself also needs protection.
why: Skin does several jobs at once. It holds water in. It feels touch. It cools you with sweat. But its biggest job is being a wall. Nothing gets in through skin that is whole. A scrape makes a hole in the wall, and that is the job it just lost.
assumes: skin covers the whole outside of you

choices: Protection from the outside environment
Keeping water inside the body
Helping the body feel touch and temperature
Helping the body cool down by sweating
rebuttals: B. Keeping water inside the body — Skin does hold water in. A small scrape lets germs in long before it dries anyone out.
C. Helping the body feel touch and temperature — Skin does feel things. The scrape did not take that away.
D. Helping the body cool down by sweating — Skin does cool the body. One small scrape does not stop the sweating.
text.call: What Job Did the Skin Lose?

title: How Might It Spread?
task: Which matching set is most sensible?
scene: The nurse gives you three short stories. Ty was near classmates who were coughing. Ana ate food that made several relatives sick. Lena touched a shared toy and rubbed her nose. Germs cannot fly or walk by themselves. Something has to carry them. Different germs travel different ways. The way it travels tells you how to stop it.
takeaway: Knowing the route helps people choose the right prevention strategy.
why: Germs do not all travel the same way. Some ride in tiny drops from a cough. Some are in food that was not cooked or kept right. Some sit on a doorknob until a hand picks them up. That is why the story matters. What somebody did tells you which way the germ came.
assumes: germs are too small to see

choices: Ty—air droplets; Ana—food route; Lena—hands/surfaces
Ty—air droplets; Ana—hands/surfaces; Lena—food route
Ty—hands/surfaces; Ana—air droplets; Lena—food route
Ty—food route; Ana—hands/surfaces; Lena—air droplets
rebuttals: B. Ty—air droplets; Ana—hands/surfaces; Lena—food route — Ana and Lena are swapped. Ana's clue was something she ate.
C. Ty—hands/surfaces; Ana—air droplets; Lena—food route — Ty and Ana are swapped. Ty was near someone who was coughing.
D. Ty—food route; Ana—hands/surfaces; Lena—air droplets — All three have moved along by one. None of them lines up with its own story.
text.setup: Ty, Ana, and Lena • Infection Control Desk

title: Handwashing Challenge
task: Put the handwashing steps in order.
scene: Lena asks why the hospital has sinks everywhere. Hands touch more things than any other body part. That makes them the busiest ride for germs. Washing lifts germs off the skin. Then the water rinses them away. It only works if you wash long enough. You also have to cover the whole hand. That is why the steps are taught in order.
takeaway: Handwashing is a simple action that can break a chain of germ spread.
why: Hands are how germs get around. Somebody touches one thing, then another, then their own face. Washing breaks that chain. Soap loosens the germs, and running water carries them away. That is why it needs both, and why the rubbing part is the part people cut short.
assumes: soap and water clean things
answerText: 1. Wet hands with clean running water. 2. Use soap and scrub all parts of the hands. 3. Rinse the soap away with clean running water. 4. Dry the hands with a clean towel or air dryer.

cards: Wet hands with clean running water.
Use soap and scrub all parts of the hands.
Rinse the soap away with clean running water.
Dry the hands with a clean towel or air dryer.

title: Same Symptom, Same Germ?
task: What is the best response?
scene: Ty and Ana both feel tired. The rest of their clues are different. So is where each of them had been. A student says they must have the same germ. The germ scientist asks you to judge that. Many different illnesses make people tired. One shared clue is weak proof. Medicine is a puzzle. The pattern across clues is what points to an answer.
takeaway: Medicine is an evidence puzzle, not a one-clue guessing game.
why: One symptom can have many causes. Lots of things make a person tired. So two tired people do not have to share a germ. You need more clues before you can say. This is a hard habit, because guessing feels faster. Saying not enough evidence yet is a real answer, not a dodge.
assumes: being tired can happen for many reasons

choices: Not enough evidence — many different problems can make a person tired.
Yes, because they were both in the same building this week.
Yes, because feeling tired is an unusual thing to report.
No, because their other clues are different, so it must be a different germ.
rebuttals: B. Yes, because they were both in the same building this week. — Being in one place is a clue worth having. Lots of people share a building and are not sick.
C. Yes, because feeling tired is an unusual thing to report. — Tired is one of the most common things people say. That is what makes it a weak clue.
D. No, because their other clues are different, so it must be a different germ. — Different clues are worth noticing. One germ can still make two people feel different things.

title: The Body Notices a Germ
task: Put the body’s germ-fighting steps in order.
scene: Ruby is getting better. The immune doctor wants to show why. Four picture cards show what her body did. The steps happen in order. Something has to be noticed before it can be fought. Helpers have to arrive before the cleanup. The last step is the surprising one. The body keeps a record of what it met.
takeaway: Immune memory can help the body respond faster when it meets the same threat again.
why: The immune system does four things, in order. A germ gets past the outside walls. Immune cells spot that something does not belong. They attack it and clear it out. Then some of them remember what it looked like. That last step is why you often do not get the same illness twice.
assumes: your body can fight off a cold
answerText: A germ gets past the body’s outside barriers. -> Immune cells notice signs that something does not belong. -> The immune system attacks the germ and helps clear it. -> Some immune cells remember important features for later.

cards: A germ gets past the body’s outside barriers.
Immune cells notice signs that something does not belong.
The immune system attacks the germ and helps clear it.
Some immune cells remember important features for later.

title: Meet the Defense Team
task: Which set is the best match?
scene: Three cards need labels. Dante has a skin shield card. Ruby has a white blood cell card. Mae has an antibody card. The body does not defend itself one way. It defends in layers. Barriers try to keep germs out. Cells patrol and attack what gets in. Special molecules know one threat very well. Each layer catches what the last one missed.
takeaway: Defense works in layers: barriers, cells, and specialized molecules.
why: Your defences are a team, and each part has one job. Skin is the wall that keeps things out. White blood cells go and find things that got in. Antibodies are the part that knows one target and sticks to it. They work together, and none of them can do the other two jobs.
assumes: a team works better than one person alone

choices: Skin—barrier; white blood cells—find/fight threats; antibodies—recognize specific targets
Skin—barrier; white blood cells—recognize specific targets; antibodies—find/fight threats
Skin—find/fight threats; white blood cells—barrier; antibodies—recognize specific targets
Skin—recognize specific targets; white blood cells—find/fight threats; antibodies—barrier
rebuttals: B. Skin—barrier; white blood cells—recognize specific targets; antibodies—find/fight threats — The last two are swapped. Antibodies are the part that knows one target.
C. Skin—find/fight threats; white blood cells—barrier; antibodies—recognize specific targets — Skin and white blood cells are swapped. Skin is a wall, not a hunter.
D. Skin—recognize specific targets; white blood cells—find/fight threats; antibodies—barrier — Skin and antibodies are swapped. Skin cannot pick out one germ from another.
text.setup: Dante, Ruby, and Mae • Pediatric Ward

title: A Vaccine Visit
task: Put the clinic process in the best order.
scene: Mae is at the clinic with her mum. A nurse will give the shot. A shot lets the body practise, so it is ready if the real germ turns up.
takeaway: The wait at the end of a vaccine visit is part of the visit: fast reactions show up in the first few minutes.
why: Check who it is first. A shot cannot be taken back. Then tell Mae what is coming, so she can hold still. Then the nurse gives it. Then you wait a few minutes. That wait is not just being polite. If a rare fast problem starts, it starts right then, and a nurse is still there.
assumes: a shot cannot be taken back once it is given
answerText: 1. Check Mae’s name and the planned vaccine with her parent. 2. Explain what will happen, so Mae can hold still. 3. The trained clinician gives the vaccine. 4. Record it, and wait a short while before leaving.

cards: Check Mae’s name and the planned vaccine with her parent.
Explain what will happen, so Mae can hold still.
The trained clinician gives the vaccine.
Record it, and wait a short while before leaving.

title: Hot or Cold Response?
task: Which explanation matches the clues?
scene: Jamal is hot after exercise. He is sweating. Ivy got caught in the rain. She is cold and shivering. Both are with the team now. The body works hard to hold one steady temperature. Cells only work well in a narrow range. When it gets too warm, the body loses heat. When it gets too cold, the body makes heat.
takeaway: Homeostasis means the body works to keep important conditions within a useful range.
why: These two do opposite things. Sweat sits on your skin and dries. Drying takes heat away with it, so you cool down. Shivering is your muscles shaking fast, and working muscles make heat. So one cools and one warms. Your body uses both to stay at about the same temperature all day.
assumes: you sweat when you are hot and shiver when you are cold

choices: Sweating helps cool; shivering uses muscle activity that helps make heat.
Sweating and shivering both make heat, because the body is trying to warm up either way.
Sweating cools by wetting the skin; shivering cools by moving air across it.
Both are signs of being unwell rather than ways of holding a steady temperature.
rebuttals: B. Both make heat, because the body is trying to warm up either way. — Shivering does make heat. Sweating does the opposite, which is the whole point.
C. Sweating cools by wetting the skin; shivering cools by moving air. — Sweating does cool. Shivering is muscles working, and working muscles make heat.
D. Both are signs of being unwell rather than ways of holding a steady temperature. — You can be unwell and do both. A healthy body does both too, every day.

title: Temperature Difference
task: How fast is her temperature rising, in degrees per hour?
scene: A chart shows two numbers for Ms. Kim. The first is 98°F. The next is 101°F. The times beside them are three hours apart.
takeaway: A change on its own is not enough; how long it took is what says whether it is fast.
why: 101 take away 98 is 3. It took 3 hours. So it went up about 1 degree each hour. That is the whole trick. One number is just a number. Two numbers and a clock make a speed. The same 3 degrees in ten minutes would be a much bigger worry.
assumes: you can take one number away from another

rebuttals: A. 1°F — 101 is three, not one, above 98.
B. 2°F — 101 is three, not two, above 98.
D. 199°F — 199 comes from adding, but the question asks for the difference.

estimate.relationship: Change each hour = how much it changed ÷ how many hours it took.

equations.e: change each hour = total change ÷ hours taken
equations.about: a rate from a change and a time

title: How Sweat Helps Cool
task: Put the simplified cooling story in order.
scene: Parker sees sweat on his arm after exercise. The nurse explains why that helps. Turning liquid water into vapour takes energy. That energy comes from the warmest thing nearby. On skin, that is the skin itself. So sweat carries heat away as it dries. It is plain physics, not magic. A breeze helps. A very humid day does not.
takeaway: The body uses physical processes, not magic, to help control temperature.
why: Sweating alone does not cool you. The drying is what cools you. Here is the order. You get warm. Sweat comes out on your skin. Some of it dries into the air. Drying needs energy, and it takes that energy as heat from your skin. That is why a wet day feels so much hotter.
assumes: water dries up in the air
answerText: The body becomes warmer during activity. -> Sweat appears on the skin. -> Some sweat evaporates into the air. -> Evaporation carries away heat and helps cool the skin.

cards: The body becomes warmer during activity.
Sweat appears on the skin.
Some sweat evaporates into the air.
Evaporation carries away heat and helps cool the skin.

title: Which Allergy Patient First?
task: Who needs the team’s immediate attention first?
scene: Three people come in with allergy signs. Sofia has itchy eyes and breathes normally. Malik has an itchy rash and talks normally. Chloe has swelling around her mouth. She is struggling to breathe. The team needs your call. An allergy is the body's defence going much too far. Most reactions stay about the same for a while. A few change very fast.
takeaway: When breathing is threatened, urgency rises sharply.
why: Swelling with trouble breathing can get dangerous in minutes. That is why Chloe goes first. Itchy eyes are horrible and they stay about the same. A big rash looks worse than a small one, but how much skin it covers is not what makes it urgent. You go by what could get worse fastest.
assumes: you cannot go long without breathing

choices: Chloe, because swelling with trouble breathing can be a medical emergency.
Sofia, because itchy eyes come first and treating them early stops the rest.
Malik, because his rash covers a large area of skin.
Whoever has been waiting longest, so the queue stays fair.
rebuttals: B. Sofia, because itchy eyes come first and treating them early stops the rest. — Itchy eyes are no fun. They do not get dangerous the way trouble breathing does.
C. Malik, because his rash covers a large area of skin. — A big rash looks worse than a small one. How much skin it covers is not what makes it urgent.
D. Whoever has been waiting longest, so the queue stays fair. — Waiting your turn is fair most places. Here the fair thing is the sickest person first.
text.setup: Sofia, Malik, and Chloe • Emergency Department

title: Allergy or Germ Clues?
task: Which comparison is most sensible?
scene: Sofia's eyes itch every spring. That is when pollen is high. She has no fever. Ty came in earlier with a fever and a cough. His classmates were sick too. The allergist asks which story sounds like an allergy. Both patients feel unwell. So no single symptom decides it. The pattern does. What else is happening, and when.
takeaway: Doctors compare patterns, timing, and exposures instead of relying on one clue.
why: Look at the pattern, not just the word. Sofia itches when the pollen comes. It happens every year. That fits an allergy. Ty has a fever. He was near people who were sick. That fits a germ. Both feel unwell. The stories under them are not the same.
assumes: some things happen at the same time every year

choices: Sofia’s repeating pollen-linked itching fits an allergy pattern; Ty’s fever plus sick contacts fits an infection pattern.
Both fit an allergy pattern, because both patients feel unwell at the same time of year.
Sofia’s itching fits an infection, because germs can make skin itch; Ty’s fever fits an allergy.
Neither pattern can be told apart until a blood test comes back.
rebuttals: B. Both fit an allergy pattern, because both patients feel unwell at the same time of year. — The season is a real clue. Ty was also near sick people, and that points somewhere else.
C. Sofia’s itching fits an infection, because germs can make skin itch; Ty’s fever fits an allergy. — The two are swapped. Itching that comes back with the pollen is the allergy pattern.
D. Neither pattern can be told apart until a blood test comes back. — A test would help. The patterns already point different ways, and that is worth saying now.

title: Emergency Team Handoff
task: Put the junior-doctor actions in order.
scene: The team is helping Chloe now. In this game you do not pick or give medicine. Your job is to get the right grown-ups fast and tell them the story.
takeaway: In an emergency the first action is the one with a clock on it, and the last is the one that protects the record.
why: Call first. That clock is running whether or not you do anything else. Then watch her breathing, because it can change fastest. Then say what she met and when. The team needs that before they act. Write it down last, so nobody has to guess the order later.
assumes: help takes time to arrive
answerText: 1. Call the emergency team, because everything else can happen while they come. 2. Stay with Chloe and watch her breathing, which is what can change fastest. 3. Tell the team what she was exposed to and when it started. 4. Write down what you saw, in the order it happened.

cards: Call the emergency team, because everything else can happen while they come.
Stay with Chloe and watch her breathing, which is what can change fastest.
Tell the team what she was exposed to and when it started.
Write down what you saw, in the order it happened.

title: Six Patients, One First Room
task: Who should go to the first available room?
scene: The waiting board is full. Nora breathes hard and cannot finish a sentence. DeShawn can walk on a sore ankle. Mei has a fever and cough but breathes fine. Mr. Alvarez feels lightheaded but is awake. Fatima has itchy eyes. Owen has a small covered scrape. One room is free. Triage asks which problem could get dangerous fastest.
takeaway: Triage means asking, “Which problem could become dangerous fastest?”
why: This is the big pattern of the whole course. Breathing trouble can get dangerous quickly, so it goes first. Feeling lightheaded is worth a look. A fever needs care. A sore ankle needs a picture. All of them are real. Only one of them is getting worse while everybody waits.
assumes: only one person can go in first

choices: Nora, because significant breathing trouble can affect the whole body quickly.
Mr. Alvarez, because feeling lightheaded could mean he is about to faint.
Mei, because a fever could spread to the other people waiting.
DeShawn, because he has been standing on a sore ankle the longest.
rebuttals: B. Mr. Alvarez, because feeling lightheaded could mean he is about to faint. — This is worth a quick check. Hard breathing is still the bigger worry.
C. Mei, because a fever could spread to the other people waiting. — A fever needs care. It does not get worse as fast as trouble breathing.
D. DeShawn, because he has been standing on a sore ankle the longest. — Waiting a long time is no fun. It does not make a sore ankle the most urgent.
text.setup: Nora, DeShawn, Mei, Mr. Alvarez, Fatima, and Owen • Central Triage

title: Send Them to the Right Place
task: Which routing set is best?
scene: Nora is with the emergency team now. Five other patients still need a next stop. A hospital is not one big room. It is a set of special places. Each one is set up to answer a certain kind of question. The right place means the right test the first time. The wrong place costs a patient hours.
takeaway: Hospitals are teams of specialized places that work together.
why: Different clues need different tools. A sore ankle needs a picture of the bone. A fever needs a check for germs. Feeling faint needs some numbers taken. Itchy eyes need an allergy check. A scrape needs the wound team. Send them all one place and most of them wait for the wrong thing.
assumes: a hospital has different rooms for different things

choices: DeShawn—Imaging/orthopedics; Mei—exam/infection evaluation; Mr. Alvarez—exam and measurements; Fatima—allergy/eye evaluation; Owen—wound-care check
DeShawn—Imaging/orthopedics; Mei—wound-care check; Mr. Alvarez—exam and measurements; Fatima—allergy/eye evaluation; Owen—exam/infection evaluation
DeShawn—wound-care check; Mei—imaging/orthopedics; Mr. Alvarez—allergy/eye evaluation; Fatima—exam and measurements; Owen—exam/infection evaluation
Send all five to the emergency team, since that is where Nora went.
rebuttals: B. DeShawn—Imaging/orthopedics; Mei—wound-care check; Mr. Alvarez—exam and measurements; Fatima—allergy/eye evaluation; Owen—exam/infection evaluation — Mei and Owen are swapped. Mei has a fever, and Owen has a scrape to clean.

C. DeShawn—wound-care check; Mei—imaging/orthopedics; Mr. Alvarez—allergy/eye evaluation; Fatima—exam and measurements; Owen—exam/infection evaluation — Almost every one is in the wrong room. A sore ankle needs a picture of the bone.
D. Send all five to the emergency team, since that is where Nora went. — The emergency team is for the most urgent patient. Five more people would slow them down.
text.setup: Five patients from the waiting board • Whole-Hospital Map
text.call: Send Them to the Right Place

title: End-of-Day Handoff
task: Put the handoff information in the best order.
scene: Your shift is ending. The evening team is arriving. They were not here for any of today. They cannot read every note in time. A handoff is a summary built for them. Who each patient is. What matters most. What has been done. What to watch for. Careful work only helps if the next person can use it.
takeaway: Science is only useful if the next person can understand and act on the evidence.
why: A handoff is for somebody who missed everything. So it starts with who and what is wrong. Then the clues you have, so they can judge for themselves. Then what has already been done, so nobody repeats it. Then what still needs doing. Get the order wrong and they hear the answer before they know the question.
assumes: the next person was not there when it happened
answerText: 1. Say who the patient is and the main problem. 2. Give the most important observations and measurements. 3. Explain what the hospital team has already done or learned. 4. State what still needs to happen next.

cards: Say who the patient is and the main problem.
Give the most important observations and measurements.
Explain what the hospital team has already done or learned.
State what still needs to happen, and who will do it.
